This something that nobody really wants done is, most often, something dead, something in stone, a monument; not something fruitful and life-giving. We would give the memorial-money—however vast a sum it may turn out to be—to the doctors, the actors, the soldiers, the sailors, willingly; to anybody!—so long as it is not given to a stone.

The truth is—when will the truth be recognised?—that the social consciousness and patriotism of this age cannot express itself in art. It is a commonplace, but a truth, to say that art is no longer municipal, but individual. In the days of Pheidias and Pericles we learn that art was municipal; the social consciousness of Athens, the imperialism or Pan-Hellenism of a Greecs recovering from the Persian wars, expressed itself wonderfully in the sculptures of the Parthenon. Flowers of lovely marble, they grew from the very roots of the nation's being—unless, indeed, you like to take the view of Thucydides, son of Melesias, that they were a sort of party-move, and that Pericles squandered on them public moneys needed as a reserve for war. Still, party or Pan-Hellenism, Pericles or Thucydides, whatever view you take, the marbles, as you gaze upon their fragments in the British Museum, seem beyond criticism. The result was perfection. What is the result of our endeavours to express our patriotism in stone?

"ARE " HOTEL-FRIENDS" DESIRABLE?

I have just returned from Switzerland, and, curiously enough, my eye fell, as soon as I opened my morning's Mirror, on several of the amusing letters you have published on the desirability or otherwise of "hotel friends."

My recent experience in Switzerland has certainly been that such friends are very charming, and I have done what "W. M." declares one never ought to do—I have written to several of them, or left them my card and address, urging them to come and see me in London.
I now read your advice and "W. M.'s" article, and am骇ed to think that I may have invited people to call upon me who, on arriving, may turn out to be ordinary bores, or worse! A. L.

I am greatly interested in the remarks on this subject made by Dora d'Espaigne Chapman, and I wish Ralph Waldo Emerson, whom your lady correspondent undoubtedly has read, could enter into the discussion.

The first reason of disappointment given in today's article is due, I think, to the fact that so few people realise that "friendship is a mutual relationship." Emerson's words, in his essay on forbearance, "Oh! be my friend, and teach me to be thine," and in his essay on compensation, "To have a friend, you must be a friend," are well worth consideration.

As regards the second reason given, his words, "Wealth without a rich heart is an ugly beggar," should suffice to turn the thought, "The rent they pay, their clothes, their ancestors and their occupations," to one of "How do they live?"

GIRLS TRAIN FOR AIR SERVICE TO GUARD U. S. COAST.

Los Angeles young women who are training for Uncle Sam's war service. They are Miss Alice La Chapelle (top); bottom, left to right: Miss Zanette Whiting; Mrs. A.B. Cochran; Mrs. William Duffy; Miss Dolores Francis; and Miss Vea Kitchin.

During death in a patriotic desire to serve the United States, six Los Angeles, Cal. young women have formed an aviation corps offering their services and their airplanes to the Government for coast patrol work.

The feminineatriots are practicing and studying the art of flying daily at the training station nearby. After a short period of instruction several of them have made successful flights to high altitudes.

Miss Alice La Chapelle, a finished aviatrix, is in charge of the girls' corps of aerial scouts, Colonel Newman; who established the first aviation corps in China, and Joseph Mattingly, a Los Angeles aviator, are instructors. Miss La Chapelle believes that she and her associates can be of valuable service to Unc/1e Sam and that when our soldiers are actively engaged fighting in Europe, the aviators will be with them, leaving the coast in serious need of patrol aviators. Their aim in forming the woman's aviation corps is to serve the government in every way possible, and filling places vacated by men called to the front.

TWO DAREDEVILS PERFORM ON ONE PLANE; FIRST TIME IN HISTORY OF AVIATDON.

Two men, their-Ams swinging in easy,stageful rhythm,performed on the unprotected wings of a plane five hundred feet above a charring crowd at the Chateau Thierry Field, Long Beach,Cal., recently. It was the first time in the history of aviation that two men, synchronizing their movements, had performed simultaneously on the same Aeroplane. Earl S. Daugherty, piloted the plane while Clarence Braguiner And Wesley May were the daredevils who performed the thrilling stunts. The exhibition was performed in the face of an Adverse wind which enhanced the danger to the Airmen. The daring stunts were filmed by an INTERNATIONAL camera man, exclusively, for INTERNATIONAL NEWS REEL exhIBitors All over the country. The photographs show the daring stunts of the Airmen.

Ivan R.Gates, San Francisco's first aero policeman, of the Police Department Aerial Patrol, delivering his prisoner, James Kelly, to Chief of Police D.A.Whits of San Francisco, at the Murina, after having transported him from Hameda, Calif., via the sky route.
